title: Coen, Farwell & Meyers on Team Growth, Competition Through Day 3 of Minicamp | Jacksonville Jaguars
text: Mini camps done now, just how much progress do you feel like the team made this week? >> Yeah, I think that over the course of the off season we've improved for sure. Um especially in the areas in which that you can improve in this time, I think we've taken steps in the right direction in terms of uh the pass game specifically. Um I think offensively um pass pro is always challenging during this time, but I think the amount of reps that we accumulated throwing the football this spring was pretty cool to see. Um guys making plays in one-on-one situations, the timing and spacing. Uh I think our defensive coverage has improved. Um guys getting a little bit uh more confident to come up and challenge people and then again that the the rush is very difficult to examine during this time, but I think Travon Walker showed up in a big way especially when we got into some competitive situations. Um doing what I challenged them with which was to dominate and through the first two days of mini camp he didn't lose many reps. So, I think we got better. >> How important are reps this time of year for guys like Caleb and Jaylen McCollum who maybe didn't get them last year? >> Yeah, huge. I mean that those guys haven't been on a on the grass in so long. So, it's valuable time. it's it's going to be a huge jump I think for those guys to come from this time to training camp. I think we'll hopefully see another step from those guys if they're going to be people that are going to help us play this season. Um I would imagine we'll see another jump because so much of this was just about getting them back out into uh calling uh making checks, calls, adjustments, and then just lining up and playing football. So, hope hopeful that those guys take another step this this summer. >> And then you talked about some guys practicing with confidence. Is Buster one of those guys that just since you've been here, you've kind of seen that confidence take over? >> Yeah, he's always kind of played and practiced with confidence. Um there's areas in which he can continue to improve. Um but I think, you know, look, we signed him to a a deal um and he comes out and just is is him. He's practiced the same way. He's approached uh the meetings and practice and games the same, you know, the same way since I've been here the whole time. So, he's consistent. He's a pro. Um I think we'll see another step from Buster this year in terms of confidence, um especially in the red zone. >> I know you usually like what you see from Trevor. But, anything stand out about this offseason? >> think that I mean, I don't know how many picks he actually threw, but I got to believe it was under five um throughout all the OTAs and mini camps. So, I think while trying to challenge himself and our receivers more with down the field passing, challenging him to um try new things of concepts and fit some play, you know, fit some throws into maybe windows you would otherwise take a check down in. Um while balancing that, I thought it did a really nice job taking care of the football, running the whole operation, um managing the protections and and some of the concepts on the field. Um yeah, I'm I'm pleased with with Trevor's spring, absolutely. >> Having John Hussey and a an officiating crew out here, how does it help? What else are they doing off the field here? >> Yeah, they've done a I mean, I don't know how many better there are than him. You know, I've I've been fortunate to be around uh John for the last 3 days and you talk about a pro's pro and and not just the experience that he has, but helping me out with uh some communication to the players. Um they did multiple presentations to our players, our rookies, our staff. And they were sat in on all the position meetings. So, they're able to answer questions live for the coaches and players. And then for me, it was like talking to them about all right, the controllable penalties versus the non-controllables. So, what can we control? And it comes down to either, you know, coaching it to happen or allowing it to happen. And so, some of that stuff we can control, some of it we can't. So, it's been great to have those guys. He's got a great crew and I think he's one of the best out there. Easy today, boy. Oh, wow. >> Yeah, first >> When asked about the unsung heroes of this lineup from this past year, one of the first names that came to mind for Trevor was yourself. Considering what you were able to accomplish on such short notice, what are your expectations for one another coming into this season? >> Just to learn as much as I can, honestly. So, they don't have to sit there and babysit me and hold my hand throughout the offense. So, I just want to learn as much as I can and honestly have the other guys play great so I can just support them for That's really all my expectations are. >> You've been around different teams this time of year. What stands out about what you guys were able to get done for the last couple of weeks? >> I mean, I would say the quality of players, I would say. I mean, cuz they all We all knew they had talent, it's a matter of working hard when you get to the league. And I feel like all our quality players really put that work in this off-season and it showed when we hit the grass. So, it was fun to be out there competing every day. >> Liam said he thinks the secondary, you know, has played well throughout this. So, what have you kind of seen from them? He said he thinks they've been sticking to him. Have you seen that competitiveness? >> Yeah, I would say so. I mean, I felt it, honestly. They They'd be around when I'm trying to get open, but it's pushed us to be better in our room. So, hopefully we just keep having that iron and sharpen iron, you know what I mean? So, >> Seeing the confidence of number seven continue to grow and it's showing up here on the practice field. >> Yeah. >> Did you see that at the end of last season continue to grow for him and how has he been different if at all this off-season? >> I mean, he's been locked in, I think. Honestly, like he He's a smart dude. I don't think he gets enough credit for how smart he is, but he is smart individual. So, I just think the longer he's around the game, the more he's in his offense, the older he gets as a man, you know, like he he's going to continue to get better and better. And I think when it really all the way click for him, I really don't see how you stop him, but good luck to whoever trying, for real. >> So, when he's going, what does that do for the rest of you guys on offense? >> Oh, it make Man, we was talking about it yesterday. Whenever BT have a good day, the whole team have a good day. You know what I mean? Like the whole team, so we all just want to keep putting that belief into him, so he know how great we think he is, and if you just half of that, we'll be okay. >> Couple of rookies in the room. What have you kind of seen about them and just how they've kind of gone about their business so far? >> Consistently made plays. And I think even before we hit the field, like they showed how smart they were. Like they were answering questions faster than us. So, we weren't surprised when they came out here and made plays. Everybody, honestly, even down to the undrafted guys. Like everybody kind of been consistent with how they catch the ball. They learn quick. They ask questions. It's been great to have them around. >> Trevor earlier in the off season talked about, hey, he's not learning any new offense cuz it's already in, but they were refining it. You might still be learning new offense. Are you? And and what does refining the offense look like out here for you? >> Just I feel like I've been in so many different systems now. It's just understanding the verbage, I would say, like pretty much teams run the same stuff. It's just what you call it. So, if I can get all the names glued down, I think that would be a big help for me, but I wouldn't say I'm learning too much. It's the same as him. I'm trying to refine it. The things I am learning really need to hold onto those, but refining for sure. >> Like the timing routes and stuff. You haven't had an off season here before, so >> I mean, that's football, though. So, I would say that part I the on-the-field part is maybe a little easier for me. Just just being in the classroom, making sure, like I said, I get the words down, so when they do call it, I don't have to stop think, "What's this in this offense?" and then go line up, you know, so >> Kind of on the How has your chemistry grown now with Trevor just being able to have an off season with him to be able to go out maybe practice on your own just things like that. >> I mean it's more so just paying attention to him. So I would say it's it's moving in the right direction like we still finding a way to make plays but the more I can pay attention to him how he move how he think what he's looking for when we run our routes I think the better we'll be so he's got to keep doing his thing and I'll catch up to wherever he is. >> What stood out about Trevor >> this this off season so far you know Liam's talked about how he's he's needed to sort of know the more advanced concepts rather than just the baseline so how's he sort of looked in your opinion? >> I mean for me personally a guy who knows the offense as well as he does like it's easy for me when I have a mistake he could just tell me right away and I can go line up and it don't take too long I can still kind of understand my job so I mean that's been great for me the way he throw the ball like he he could tell you exactly where he's thinking and we could tell him exactly what we's thinking so the communication that helped the leadership he's been doing a good job this year. >> I don't know how how much you've seen it but just or how much you've thought about it but Brian Thomas just seeing what he's been able to do on the field over the last few days over the last few weeks how impressed have you been? >> Super impressed but I mean I was already I was impressed with BT from a distance just getting here is kind of what the expectation was of him but he just I mean it's just it's fun watching him play honestly so it's just great to have him I'm happy on our team and he helping us out so. >> How dangerous is is a guy like that when he has the confidence when he's making the plays when he's doing things consistently? >> As dangerous as he want to be honestly I think he that type of player like if he decide that he want to be great that day and he commit to it and he will be great that day. >> So. >> For sure. >> Thanks Tony. >> Thanks you Tony. >> Yes. >> Um. Heath obviously you have a bunch of new rookies this year just in terms of what you've seen from them on special teams you know Liam's talked about how much you guys emphasize that and what whenever you draft anybody but just how have you seen the the rookie class progress? >> It's been great. It's been a good off season. They really bought in right when they got here. I think it's you know, it's a work in progress as far as where they're at. But they're putting in the time. They're learning the drills and that's what this off season's about is getting them prepped to to to compete in training camp. So they've been they've done a really really good job of buying in and kind of seeing it and a lot of these guys haven't played a ton of special teams since earlier in their college careers. So a lot of this stuff's new. But they're getting better every day and and to see this last you know, few you know, two weeks they've really taken a big step you know, in their in in their production. >> He's only been practicing in full this week. But in terms of where you guys envision him punt returner, can he return kicks in terms of where he fits in on that side of the ball? >> I mean, I think he's going to be a really really good kick returner. He can punt return as well. You know, fortunately obviously we have Parker. We have guys to punt return. But yeah, Josh has been really really good. I think in all phases probably the best way to say it. He's I plan on playing four phases. He's going to be a good player for us. I was excited to get to to be able to draft him. He was one of my favorites watching him. So and and he and he's showcasing what he can do not only as a receiver but you know, for me as well. >> So how would you evaluate that knowing Parker potentially having a little bit more of an elevated role on offense? I know you don't want to lose him at that punt returner spot. But how would you evaluate that competition? >> I mean, I think like you said, I love Parker back there. I think we'll just have to see how that plays out you know, with the roster and how that looks come week one. And it may be you know, it may be changing throughout the season. There may be games when you know, we we need a big play and and and he's back there and there's other times when we'll provide a big play from somebody else. So I think Parker's back there as a punt returner if we can. But we're going to make great decisions as a team, as an organization. If If is the you know, he the top target for us as he as I had imagined he will be, you know, what does that look like for special teams? We'll figure it out, but we have plenty of guys that can return. We have a good group. So, I'm I'm confident and comfortable where we're at if it's not Parker. >> Did you take note of the UFL's 60-yard field goals, four points? And what do you think about that? >> I'd love it. You know, that'd be a cool cool little bonus if you could get a an extra, you know, an extra point out of that. So, yeah, I think it'd be a good little interesting thing for the kickers that can do it. And you know, maybe with our guy, maybe make it a a five-pointer. >> We can get a 70. Let's get a 75-pointer. >> I mean, it wouldn't surprise me. You know, I mean, our guy can do them. There's several kickers across the league, I believe, that can do them. Yeah, I think it could happen very easily. The guys are getting stronger and and and and and more talented as the as the year goes on. And so, yeah, it wouldn't surprise me. Do you think maybe at some point the league's going to go, "Higher crossbar, narrower, you know, something." Anything? >> I don't believe so. I mean, I think that's down the road. I think it's really cool to see these long kicks. Uh you know, it's you know, it's cool thing to see when you're seeing you're in field goal range, but you're on the other side of the 50. You know, other game management guys, they're aware of Cam. And that's a that's a weapon. That's a cool thing that we can potentially be in range and send them out there, you know, even on the on the other side of the 50. title: Isaiah Rodgers & Ivan Pace Jr. Address the Media Following Vikings Minicamp Practice
text: Now that the off-season program is complete, how much was accomplished? >> I think a lot was accomplished. I think it brought us together. A lot of guys like 100% OTA uh participation. So, I think that's definitely brought us closer. >> Think about your situation, where you are now in terms of this defense compared to this time last year. Is it night and day? >> A lot more clarity for me. You know, I came in last year and I was kind of getting the gloves on the defense, trying to understand, you know, how they led the league in interceptions and things like that. So, I think coming in now and you know, speaking with the coaches and the coaching staff and you know, having Murphy in my corner and Ford-Stewart and Deal, I think those guys definitely made it a lot easier for me this year. >> How much have you felt like that you've found a home? I mean, I know you're in a contract here, but how much would you like to be here long-term? >> Oh, I said it last year, yeah. I'm not trying to go nowhere, if we're being honest. I think it's a perfect place for me, for for my family. So, you know, just you know, the great fans, you know, I I built a lot of relationship with a lot of people outside and you know, the pre-game uh you know, ball toss and things like that. So, those things I want to continue doing. >> Is there any progress in terms of a contract extension? >> No, I'm here to play ball. So, whatever happens happens, but regardless if it happens or not, I'm here to play ball. >> The way last year ended for you guys, yeah, ending on a five-game winning streak, but not making the playoffs. How does that motivate you? How does that motivate the group? >> Uh five-game winning streak ending out which is pretty cool, but you know, that was all for the fans. You know, we just want to show them, you know, what we can potentially be for this year, upcoming years, but I think last year is behind us. I think we got to just all reset, all starts with the new game one. >> James Pierre, what does he bring to the defense? >> He's physical. He's a dog. He's ready to hit. We're already talking about what he's going to do when he puts his pads on. So, I'm ready to see him, you know, see him out there. >> What do these next few weeks look like? So, training camp starts in what, five, six weeks? What will you be doing in terms of on the field these next five, six weeks? >> Uh really just focusing on just keeping my body, you know, intact with the season. You know, I don't want to come back and have to try to get back in shape and things like that. Just keeping, you know, just keep my body accustomed to what I'm going to potentially be doing throughout the whole season. >> I mean, now that the off-season program is complete, how much has been accomplished the last what, seven, eight weeks? >> Uh just building this team, working together on the defense. Uh yeah. Uh, just everybody getting back in here and working out and learning a new defense and got the young guys in here. So, it's good. >> You say learning the new defense. I mean, it's a defense you're very familiar with. So, what do you mean by that? >> I was saying like learning for the new rookies, like teaching them and helping them out. You know what I'm saying? >> Is it crazy to think about that you're now one of those vets trying to teach the rookies? >> Yeah, it is. What I'm going to year four? It's crazy. Go fast. >> Yeah, I mean, does the cliche hold true that time flies? Does it feel like it's already year four? >> No, I don't even feel like it's year four. I look back and then I thought I was a rookie last year, but it's fun. >> How do you evaluate your first three years? >> Um, it was pretty good for the most part. Just got to keep growing and keep learning and keep figuring everything out. >> All right, well, what does that look like? So, what does that finished product look like in your mind? What sort of step do you want to take this year? >> Uh, just trying to be a leader for everybody and yeah.

title: WORRY NOT: Jay Ward Can Replace Harrison Smith For Minnesota Vikings
text: I don't know if Harrison Smith is going to retire or not, but I do know that Jay Ward can step up to the mantle. >> You are Locked On Vikings. Your daily Minnesota Vikings [music] podcast, part of the Locked On Podcast Network. Your team every day. >> What's going on everybody? Welcome to the Locked On Vikings podcast where we're always trying to learn something new. It's part of the Locked On Podcast Network, the number one sports podcasting network and today on the show I want to dump a little bit of safety knowledge. Uh this has been a big project that I'm going to talk about in a lot more detail uh throughout the off season as it comes up, but I really wanted to have an idea of how I felt if Harrison Smith comes back or if he doesn't. So, if you've been living under a rock, Harrison Smith, he's been released from the Vikings. He's also technically a free agent. Uh it's everybody's understanding that if he does come back, he would come back and resign a new deal with the Vikings. He's not going to go sign with the Panthers or whatever, but he could if he wanted to. But if he does or does not come back is the real question. Will he retire or will he come back to the Vikings and say, "Let's work out a another deal?" And I don't know the answer to this at this point. I I have genuinely heard both publicly and privately both sides of this of where it's going to be. So, I am in a blender on this one. Your guess is as good as mine. So, the first thing I want to do is the math on what it looks like with and without him, what is needed with and without him. I want to speak a little bit on Josh Metellus and a little bit on Jay Ward and maybe a longer one on Jay Ward like next week if we really want to because here's the deal. The take is that I think Jay Ward can do the Harrison Smith role. If Harrison Smith's Smith leaves, it's you know what? I should take that back. Joshua Metellus does the Harrison Smith role. Jay Ward does the Joshua Metellus role. That's what I think the best thing is based on the tape from last year. That's just one podcaster's opinion. That's where I'm at. But it functionally it means Jay Ward is replacing Harrison Smith, but really we're shuffling some stuff around to make it work out. And that also is a world where we don't necessarily need to ask a lot of Theo Jackson if he's around, and we don't need to ask anything of Jacoby Thomas if we don't want to. He's the wild card in all this. I have no idea what to expect from or where to slot him in. But of course, if he proves to be a valuable asset, that makes a bunch of this stuff easier. But I'm not banking on it the way that I'm putting this down. He can redshirt if he has to. All the options are open there. Put a pin in it, set it aside. let's do the math here, right? If Harrison Smith does come back, you've got him doing the role he usually does, which is going to be a little bit of deep safety, a little bit of the box, you know, he's going to do um that kind of classic thing that that he does mostly in inner quarters. You're never going to ask him to be the guy that uh moves all the way over across the field. You're not going to ask for huge uh like huge rangy plays out of him anymore, and they haven't. And you're going to get somebody who's, you know, smart enough, who can get everybody aligned, who can still be valuable on the on the line of scrimmage and stuff like that. There is, I think, a limit to that where that did not exist in the previous years just because Harrison Smith is getting up there. We saw a few times last year where he couldn't break on the ball the way he used to, and then he was late. Um or times where he couldn't get off the snap as quick as he used to, and it was just a little bit too late to get to the quarterback, right? Sometimes that's just good on the quarterback for getting the ball out, but still, right? There's still going to be like a limit to that. Earlier this season, I did a show where I kind of named all the Brian Flores roles. And in terms of the safety room, I described Metellus, I gave him the name Rover. I'm just making up words here and I just thought it would be good to have a common language we could use. So, we'll talk about a Rover position. When you hear Rover, think the stuff Josh Metellus does, where he can bump over to a linebacker alignment if he has to, or bump out to be a slot corner if he has to, or to be like an apex overhang that's just kind of like out in the ocean on the alignment if he has to, and he can also play like true traditional safety, deep half, deep third, that kind of thing. And then I named the Cam Bynum, Theo Jackson, I named that the fire. Cuz you got to run around with your hair on fire. That is a more rangy safety. That is you're pretty much banished to deep. You're going to blitz some cuz everybody blitzes some, nobody doesn't blitz, but you're going to blitz like less than everybody else and you're going to mostly be about coverage. You're not going to be asked as often to get into the run fit. In this job, for most of the season, Theo Jackson and Jay Ward traded reps. And over the course of the year, Jay Ward started getting more and more and Theo Jackson started getting less and less for reasons that now that I've really watched it in depth and applied a lot of the knowledge that I got from just asking around and for the draft and the research that I did for the draft to just try to learn safety a little bit better and then going back and applying that knowledge is kind of why I'm revisiting this topic. I can see exactly what was going on here, why Theo Jackson kind of lost that and why Jay Ward got it. And then the Harrison Smith role I've been calling the shooter because this is a guy that you often want to have on the weak side, so the side with fewer passing strengths because you want them to be poaching on the strong side of three by one, right? You You want them to take those crossers. That's so that you're going to have them there often. Obviously, you only have so much control over it with motion and all the pre-snap stuff and alignment tricks that that teams have these days. Um, but that's been the Harrison Smith role. And then that that fire role, that's with Theo Jackson and Jay Ward, think about that as like what Cam Bynum did before. So, if you want to think of this in terms of like Metellus, Bynum, and Smith, those are the words I'm going to use. Okay. So, Harrison Smith comes back. We put him back in that shooter role. He's going to be on the weak side. He's going to be poaching stuff. He's going to be blitzing. Uh you know, we're going to have all kinds of fun with that. We put Metellus in his same role, the rover. He's going to be all over the formation. And then what do you do with that fire? Right? I guess it's Jay Ward and Theo Jackson uh compete for it. And Jacobi Thomas is maybe in there, too. And and actually in that world, I'm not going to count out Jacobi Thomas based on his college tape. Uh I I actually think that that role is a pretty good fit for him. I I think he can do that as somebody that's maybe not going to be in the box as much. If I recall, I liked that and and I was kind of on an island there where I didn't find him to be the the the best run-fit player, blitz player, all that stuff. He could do it. He could be part of it. But I kind of preferred him on the back end making range plays. And that's what that fire role is. So, I would love that. If he could win that job, you have this nice dynamic three-way competition. We're all happy, right? That works fine. If Harrison Smith does not come back, it gets a little bit spicier. Because that that same shooter role is a difficult one. And I honest-to-god think that Josh Metellus is the only person we can trust at any of these three roles. I can't trust Theo Jackson in that fire role. And I I don't know if he's the quite the physical kind of player you want as the in those box roles or playing slot corner or anything like that. That's never been the kind of athlete Vikings have asked him to be. And what do you get out of Jay Ward? Well, I'll talk about what I like about Jay Ward in some of these places a little later. But for Jay Ward, that fire role I think is a waste of a lot of what made him kind of pop at the end of the year. Um if if you recall those last three games, Jay Ward got a lot more run, and he made a bunch of plays. He made a bunch of interesting plays in the run against the Giants. He had some cool blitzes and some really good physical play against the Lions, and kind of popped off. And we went, "Whoa, whoa, whoa. What's this?" I did a whole Patreon video about it. title: Dan Duggan Recaps Giants Mini Camp | 162
text: Welcome to Giants Nation. I'm your host, Bobby Skinner, and today we've got Dan Dugen of The Athletic, defending Tony Award winner, two-time Tony Award winner on the show talking about mini camp OTAAS now that it's completely off, you know, you have this six week break. Um, so just like everything we saw this summer leading us into training camp. So, always a good interview with Doug and he's always insightful, always a good conversation. Um, now that mini camp is over, there wasn't really anything that big that came out of it specifically that like, oh, these are the things that we learned from OTAAS and mini camp, right? I mean, one got clouded by all the political stuff with Darden and Abdul Carter. One was the Odell stuff. Um, but you did get to talk to positional coaches. Wasn't a lot of takeaways I had from it. You know, these the first time these guys get interviewed, they get asked about specific players and it's just kind of a lot of like, oh yeah, this guy's doing great. He's really bought in. and his mindset's different. Um, you know, clean slate type of stuff. There was like, you know, I'll kind of scroll through a couple things that I I thought that I I liked was the uh running back coach Willie Tagert, who has been with the Harboss for a long time, uh, was basically like, what makes the Harboss work? And he's like, there's a forcefulness and sincerity, right? Like there's there's they're hard asses, but there was also sincerity to connect with the players. He's like, you rarely get both, right? you either get like the players coaches who's trying to connect with you or just you know the drill sergeant and Harbaugh gives you a little bit of both. So I thought that was interesting. Uh Charlie Bullan and he's talked about this before but talked about like hey with pass rushing you got to have that power element to have consistency. There was that and then I thought Brian Callahan actually had the best one. A lot of times the quarterback coach is the most actually O line coach is usually the most desired you know interview. Uh, but I thought Brian Callahan was like was pretty good. He's like, "Yeah, we're kind of, you know, letting him make corre like, you know, like he he Dart has a good ability to take coaching, make corrections, make mistakes, and then fix them." Um, which I think we have seen, me and Dougen actually talked about that a little bit because Dougen says in the interview like Dart has kind of struggled in these OTAAS in mini camp, but we referenced last year where it's like there was actually like gradual progression in training camp. You rarely don't see that. obviously a young quarterback, so those are very different than any other position. Um, but talked about letting him like do things his way. You know, some I guess there's like things that you look for is like one thing I was looking for in this training camp was were they going to change up Jackson Dart's uh shotgun stance. Uh because the large m uh Brian Callahan with Cam Ward, uh Matt Nai with the Chiefs and Patrick Mahomes and then even Greg Roman last year with the Chargers, they all had their quarterbacks with left foot back, right? And that's trying to like get the timing right with their quick game and stuff. Um Dart's a right foot back guy. They're letting Dart stay right foot back. So like that's something that we learned and I'm glad that they're letting him stay with that. the more you hear from quarterbacks, it's very much like you should stay with what you've been doing. Jones changed the first year of Dable and Dable. So Dable changed Jones. He didn't change Darts, which makes me think that Dart probably was a little more strong willed. Like, no, this is the way I'm comfortable. This is the way I'm going to play. I guess the biggest thing to come out of OTAS and mini camps to me that's is the kicker situation, right? The fact that they cut Jason Sanders, which assumably, you know, he wasn't doing very well. John Harbaugh kind of made it, you know, said it in a nice way like, yeah, he doesn't really have what it takes to, you know, be a kicker in this area, which is basically like he's he's been flat out bad. title: Aldon Smith passes away at 36
text: Coming to you with tremendously sad news. The 49ers have just announced that Aldon Smith, their former pass rusher who took the league by storm in 2011 and 2012, the start of the Jim Harbaugh era, league record 33 and 1/2 sacks over those two seasons, has passed away at the age of 36. The 49ers released this statement. Reads, "We are devastated by the sudden and tragic passing of Aldon Smith. Aldon's undeniable talent and sheer dominance on the field were on display from the moment he joined our organization, having recorded one of the best rookie seasons the National Football League has ever seen. Beyond his excellence as a player, Aldon will be remembered for his infectious smile that lit up every room he walked into. Our entire organization sends its deepest condolences to the Smith family and all who knew and loved Aldon." I'm sure that most watching this know why his tenure with the 49ers ended. There was a legal a litany of legal troubles that eventually pushed Aldon Smith from the 49ers and beyond that out of the NFL. He played for the Raiders in 2015 after the 49ers cut him, and then he returned to the league after a 4-year hiatus and played for the Cowboys in 2020. But that was it for Aldon Smith, and it remains one of the biggest what if stories in NFL history because of the talent that he showcased early on. 14 sacks his rookie year, 19 and 1/2 sacks in 2012, his second season. He was on a Hall of Fame trajectory from the beginning. Obviously, that derailed and now he has passed away. We have no further confirmed details and you guys know that I I'm not going to get into speculation, especially in a situation like this, but we can say that this is absolutely tragic and I'm sure very, very sad for a lot of the fans who enjoyed watching Aldon Smith play for the 49ers between 2011 and 2014. This news came across just a few minutes ago. We're going to have an article up on the San Francisco Standard soon. I'll bring you updates as we learn more over time. But, you know, I'm 38. title: Browns can’t expect Deshaun Watson to be healthy for full season | Pro Football Talk | NFL on NBC
text: In Cleveland, they they have a lot of quarterbacks. They have more quarterbacks than doors in the facility. They wrapped up a three-day mini camp on Thursday. And they don't know who their quarterback's going to be either. It looked like it was going to be Deshaun Watson early, Michael. It feels like Shedeur Sanders has made some strides. My theory is that somebody had a a fairly pointed talk with him about all the things he needs to do. It's not just about game day. There's a lot of other stuff you have to do to properly prepare yourself and properly lead a football team. You can't just show up and play like Brett Favre always wanted to do. Brett Favre didn't want to do anything but show up and play. I think someone has convinced him he needs to pay attention to details and needs to do a lot of these other things and embrace it as part of this day in and day out grind and it may give him a shot to win the job over Deshaun Watson. >> Yeah, I think even if he doesn't win the job over Watson, Mike, I think he is somebody who should prepare to play and he should prepare to play a lot. Because if you look at Watson his time in Cleveland, after a while it's just not a coincidence. It's just something that you know, his he's been through so many injuries. Uh the last three to four years. If you just list the Deshaun Watson injuries, it it it would seem like his body is 45 years old. Yeah, it's surprising that he's not as old as people think he is. Because he has been he's been off the radar for a while. Uh he's had major injuries the last four years. You just look at him and say, "Even if he wins the job, the Browns would be foolish to think, okay, he's got the job and we're going to plan on having Deshaun Watson be our quarterback for 17 games." It's it's very unlikely. So, I think to your point, Shedeur really does have to be on his details because the Browns are going to need him. He's going to get some time. It's likely he's going to get some time as the backup. >> Yeah, Watson said earlier this week it's the first time he's been fully healthy since week three of the 2023 season, which is encouraging but also discouraging because and I'm saying this to Devin the other day, one of the reasons I have so much respect for professional football players, you spend so much time and effort getting your body into peak 100% physical condition so you can go out and get it injured and do it all over again. And that's the reality. How long is Deshaun Watson going to stay healthy? It reminds me of one of the original criticisms Chris had of Watson that he treats every play like it's the last play of the Super Bowl. You have to know when to give up. You have to know when to call it quits. You can't put yourself and he gets hit a lot and you know, I know a lot of quarterbacks get hit a lot and with him it hasn't been the narrative that's become for certain others like hey, why don't you slide? Why don't you get out of bounds? You know, the Jackson Dart stuff, but when you look at how injured Deshaun Watson has been, there is a point where you got to pull the plug on a play. All right, here's Todd Monken, head coach of the Browns, on the improvement that he has witnessed in second-year quarterback Shedeur Sanders. >> I just think he's doing a better job. I think he's being more decisive. Now, it's easy to say we're not in pads. It just feels like he's making quicker decisions. The ball's coming out of his hands, which he's going to have to do. Not that he doesn't have play making ability cuz he does, but his ability to process quicker and get the ball out of his hands and eliminate lost yardage plays is going to be huge for us to be able to stack plays and score, which is ultimately the number one thing to do. >> You know, my take on all of this and I'm sure we've encountered someone like this at some point in our lives, mainly professional lives. Somebody who knows how to do the hard parts of the job, but keeps tripping over their shoelaces on the easy parts of the job. And I kind of feel like that's what the Browns think and what Monken may think of Shedeur. He has play-making ability. He can do the hard parts of the job. We just got to get him to do the easy parts of the job. Because if he can master the easy parts of the job, he'll be even better on the hard parts of the job. >> Yeah, and and I wonder it why the easy parts, and this is you're right, we've all worked with somebody like that. And the question we have, whether it's uh whe- whether it's football or or school or any other uh industry or profession, we say, "Why are the easy parts difficult for you?" And a lot of times the easy things are difficult because that person thinks it's boring. They're bored by the easy stuff. They like the the drama. They like the the big things. They like the hard things, but the the mundane things, they get bored by them. I don't know if that's what's happening with Shedeur Sanders, uh but as a quarterback, y- you know, your your success is embracing the boring things. Hey, sometimes you got to go Hey, that check down. Sometimes it's throwing the ball away and living to see another play. And so, he's got to he's got to master that, and I guess if he can master that, maybe he will win that job. But that's what I think that's what Todd Monken is looking for. >> And the challenge is, and it's a combination of maturity and just understanding all those boring things make the exciting things even more exciting. You convince him you'll be better. Gets back to what we were talking about. Good coaches, you find a way to press the buttons and get the desired result. All right, it's Mike Florio.
